what.text: Ipamorelin is a lab-made chain of five amino acids (Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2), including amino acids not found in nature. Novo Nordisk scientists described it in 1998.

src.label: Raun et al., Eur J Endocrinol, 1998
FDA, bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks (Category 2 page)

what.text: It is a growth hormone secretagogue: it acts on the ghrelin receptor in the pituitary to release growth hormone. In pigs, unlike GHRP-6 and GHRP-2, it did not raise the stress hormones ACTH and cortisol, even at very high doses.

src.label: Raun et al., Eur J Endocrinol, 1998

what.text: In healthy men given it by vein, it caused one burst of growth hormone, peaking at about 40 minutes. Its half-life was about 2 hours.

src.label: Gobburu et al., Pharm Res, 1999

what.text: Ipamorelin is not an approved medicine anywhere we checked. Using it for sleep has not been studied.

research.text: Ipamorelin was tested in people as a treatment for slow bowel recovery after surgery (postoperative ileus). The published Phase II trial found no significant benefit over placebo. We found no study of ipamorelin and sleep.
Each study is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Healthy men, by vein, 1999

facts.v: dose-escalation study; five infusion rates, each given over 15 minutes. No placebo group in the abstract.
healthy men, 8 at each of 5 dose levels

research.found: Growth hormone rose at every dose, in a single burst that faded to negligible levels. Levels of the drug rose in proportion to the dose. Half-life was about 2 hours.

src.label: Gobburu et al., Pharm Res, 1999

research.title: Bowel surgery recovery, Helsinn trial 201

facts.v: multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase II (NCT00672074), sponsored by Helsinn Therapeutics
117 adults having small or large bowel resection
infusions by vein twice daily from day 1 after surgery, up to 7 days or discharge
time to tolerating a solid meal; adverse events and lab tests

research.found: Median time to the first tolerated meal was 25.3 hours with ipamorelin and 32.6 hours with placebo, which was not a significant difference. Adverse events occurred in 87.5% on ipamorelin and 94.8% on placebo.

src.label: Beck et al., Int J Colorectal Dis, 2014
NCT00672074, ClinicalTrials.gov

research.title: Bowel surgery recovery, dose-finding trial

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding Phase II (NCT01280344), sponsored by Helsinn Therapeutics
320 adults aged 18 to 85 after open partial bowel resection

research.found: The registry lists the trial as completed in May 2014. No results are posted, and we found no published paper.

src.label: NCT01280344, ClinicalTrials.gov

research.text: In rats after abdominal surgery, repeated ipamorelin infusions increased stool output, food intake and weight gain. In rats and pigs it released growth hormone with similar strength to GHRP-6. These results are in animals only.

us.text: Not FDA approved for any use. FDA placed ipamorelin acetate in Category 2 for outsourcing facilities (503B) on September 29, 2023, because it may present significant safety risks. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none. A search of Drugs@FDA found no product with ipamorelin as an active ingredient.

items.text: ipamorelin acetate was added on September 29, 2023. FDA says compounded ipamorelin acetate "may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation or peptide-related impurities" and contains unnatural amino acids that make it harder to characterize. FDA adds: "A study published in literature identified serious adverse events including death when ipamorelin was administered intravenously for improving gastric motility."

world.lead: Ipamorelin is not approved as a medicine in any country we checked. FDA lists it as a compounding safety risk, Canada has seized it, Australia makes it prescription-only, and WADA bans it at all times.

countries.status: Not approved. In FDA's compounding Category 2 for outsourcing facilities (503B) since Sept 29, 2023.

after.text: Ipamorelin is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) under WADA class S2.2.4, growth hormone releasing factors. The class names "growth hormone secretagogues (GHS) and their mimetics [e.g. anamorelin, capromorelin, ibutamoren (MK-677), ipamorelin, lenomorelin (ghrelin), macimorelin and tabimorelin]." All substances in class S2 are non-Specified. It is still named in the same class on the 2027 list, which takes effect January 1, 2027.

side.text: The safety data come mostly from two bowel-surgery trials, where it was given by vein. FDA says a published study reported serious adverse events, including death.

items.text: FDA says "a study published in literature identified serious adverse events including death when ipamorelin was administered intravenously for improving gastric motility," and that it has no safety information for some other injection routes.

unconfirmed: We could not open the full text of the study FDA cites for serious adverse events including death; the abstract of the published Phase II trial does not mention deaths.
The second Helsinn Phase II trial (NCT01280344, 320 people) has no posted or published results that we could find.
We could not confirm whether ipamorelin's development for bowel recovery has been stopped.
Status in the UK was not checked against a regulator record.
surprises: Ipamorelin was developed as a selective growth hormone releaser; its only Phase II results, for bowel recovery after surgery, showed no significant benefit over placebo.
FDA's Category 2 entry cites serious adverse events including death in a published intravenous study, while the trial abstract calls the drug well tolerated.
We found no study of ipamorelin and sleep.
